title: Adams' Synchronological Chart of Universal History
summary: Sebastian C. Adams's 23-foot wall chart of the world's history from Creation to the 1870s: the Bible's family lines along the top, the nations as streams of color below, and hundreds of small pictures of the people, buildings and inventions of every age.

about:
## About the chart

Sebastian C. Adams, a teacher and Presbyterian minister in Oregon, first published this chart in 1871 as a *Chronological Chart of Ancient, Modern and Biblical History*. It sets 6,000 years of history side by side on one long sheet, about 23 feet wide, so that a reader can see at a glance what was happening everywhere in the world at the same time. That is what *synchronological* means.

The stream of time runs from left to right. Upright pillars mark each hundred years and thinner red lines the decades. The Bible's family lines, from Adam through Noah, Abraham and David to Jesus, run along the top. Below them each nation flows as a band of color, widening as it grows, splitting when it divides and ending when it is conquered. Small pictures stand beside the streams: the pyramids, the Tower of Babel, the kings and prophets, the printing press, the steam engine.

## Reading its dates

Adams based every date on the system of Archbishop James Ussher, who in the 1650s counted back through the Bible's genealogies and reached 4004 BC for Creation and 2348 BC for the Flood. Adams explains that he kept Ussher's system because most of the dates in the history books of his day were built on it, while saying plainly that "Moses assigns no date to this Creation."

Read the chart as a picture of how a 19th-century Christian historian saw the whole of history, not as the last word on its dates. Many Christians still hold a young earth and a chronology close to Ussher's. Others, together with most historians and archaeologists today, place Egypt's early kings, the first cities and the earth itself much earlier, and read the genealogies of Genesis as not meant to be added up into a calendar. The topic [Dating the Kings](/topic/regnal-chronology) shows how the dates of Israel's and Judah's kings are worked out today.

## Using this page

Drag the chart to move along it; scroll, pinch or use the buttons to zoom in until the smallest writing is clear. Each colored mark is something the collection has linked: open it to read about it, go to the passage in the books here, or read more on Wikipedia. The list below the chart has the same marks in the chart's order, and *Go to* takes you to any year.
